140: Preview
141: This feature is
142: subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the

144: Terms.
145: Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support.
146: For more information, see the
147: launch stage descriptions.
148: Gemini Notebook Enterprise is a powerful tool for generating insights and
149: summaries from your documents. This page describes the APIs that let you
150: perform the following notebook management tasks programmatically:
151: Create a notebook
152: Retrieve a notebook
153: List recently viewed notebooks
154: Delete a notebook
155: Share a notebook
156: Before you begin
157: Before you start working with your notebooks, do the following:
158: Set up Gemini Notebook Enterprise.
159: Get licenses for Gemini Notebook Enterprise
160: and assign a license to your user account.
161: Grant the Cloud NotebookLM User role
162: (roles/discoveryengine.notebookLmUser) to your user account.
163: In a local terminal or Cloud Shell, sign in to the
164: Google Cloud CLI with your user credentials by running
165: the gcloud auth login command:
166: gcloud auth login
167: Signing in with your user credentials ensures that
168: gcloud auth print-access-token generates an access token for your user
169: account. The projects.locations.notebooks REST
170: API methods on
171: this page require an authenticated user account with an active
172: Gemini Notebook Enterprise license.
173: Use the US multi-regional endpoint
174: If your Gemini Notebook Enterprise subscription is in the US
175: multi-region, you can send the requests on this page to the US multi-regional
176: endpoint, discoveryengine.us.rep.googleapis.com. A multi-regional endpoint
177: processes your requests and terminates TLS within the multi-region, so your
178: request data stays in the US while it's in transit. Using this endpoint doesn't
179: change where your notebooks are stored. For more information, see
180: Regional and multi-regional API endpoints
181: overview in the Google Cloud
182: security guide.
183: To use the US multi-regional endpoint, make the following changes to each
184: request URL on this page:
185: Replace the
186: ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com
187: host with discoveryengine.us.rep.googleapis.com.
188: Set LOCATION to us.
189: The rest of each request stays the same. To learn how you choose your
190: subscription's multi-region, see
191: Get a subscription.
192: For the list of regional and multi-regional service endpoints, see
193: Regional and multi-regional service endpoints
194: in the Virtual Private Cloud guide.
195: Create a notebook
196: To create a new notebook, use the
197: notebooks.create
198: method.
199: REST
200: curl -X POST \
201: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
202: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
203: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks" \
204: -d '{
205: "title": "NOTEBOOK_TITLE",
206: }'
207: Replace the following:
208: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
209: values:
210: us for the US multi-region
211: eu for the EU multi-region
212: global for the Global location
213: For more information, see
214: Specify a multi-region
215: for your data store.
216: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
217: LOCATION:
218: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
219: For more information, see Locations.
220: NOTEBOOK_TITLE: a UTF-8 encoded string used as a
221: title for the notebook that you want to create.
222: If the request is successful, you should receive a JSON similar to the
223: following.
224: {
225: "title": "NOTEBOOK_TITLE",
226: "notebookId": "NOTEBOOK_ID",
227: "emoji": "",
228: "metadata": {
229: "userRole": "PROJECT_ROLE_OWNER",
230: "isShared": false,
231: "isShareable": true
232: },
233: "name": "NOTEBOOK_NAME"
234: }
235: Note the following:
236: NOTEBOOK_ID: a unique ID to identify
237: the created notebook. You need the notebook ID for other notebook management
238: tasks, such as sharing or retrieving.
239: NOTEBOOK_NAME: the complete resource name of the
240: notebook. This field has the following pattern:
241: projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID
242: Access the created notebook and get its ID in a browser
243: To access the created notebook and get its ID using a browser, do the following.
244: Go to the Gemini Notebook Enterprise homepage that's available at one of
245: the following URLs:
246: If you're using a Google identity, go to:
247: https://notebook.cloud.google.com/LOCATION/?project=PROJECT_NUMBER
248: If you're using a third-party identity, go to:
249: https://notebook.cloud.google/LOCATION/?project=PROJECT_NUMBER
250: Select the created notebook. The URL of the selected notebook has the following pattern:
251: If you're using a Google identity:
252: https://notebook.cloud.google.com/LOCATION/notebook/NOTEBOOK_ID?project=PROJECT_NUMBER
253: If you're using a third-party identity:
254: https://notebook.cloud.google/LOCATION/notebook/NOTEBOOK_ID?project=PROJECT_NUMBER
255: Note the URL and the notebook ID, which are useful for other notebook
256: management tasks, such as sharing.
257: Retrieve a notebook
258: To retrieve a specific notebook using its notebook ID, use the
259: notebooks.get
260: method.
261: REST
262: curl -X GET \
263: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
264: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
265: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID"
266: Replace the following:
267: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
268: values:
269: us for the US multi-region
270: eu for the EU multi-region
271: global for the Global location
272: For more information, see
273: Specify a multi-region
274: for your data store.
275: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
276: LOCATION:
277: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
278: For more information, see Locations.
279: NOTEBOOK_ID: the notebook's unique identifier
280: that you received when you created the notebook.
281: If the request is successful, you should get a JSON response similar to the
282: following for an empty notebook. If you call this method after you
283: add sources to your notebook, you
284: receive details about all the sources added to the retrieved notebook. If you
285: have configured CMEK
286: details,
287: you also receive CMEK-related information for the notebook.
288: {
289: "title": "NOTEBOOK_TITLE",
290: "notebookId": "NOTEBOOK_ID",
291: "emoji": "",
292: "metadata": {
293: "userRole": "PROJECT_ROLE_OWNER",
294: "isShared": false,
295: "isShareable": true,
296: "lastViewed": "LAST_VIEWED_TIME",
297: "createTime": "LAST_CREATED_TIME"
298: },
299: "name": "NOTEBOOK_NAME"
300: }
301: List recently viewed notebooks
302: To get a list of all notebooks in a project that were recently viewed, use the
303: notebooks.listRecentlyViewed
304: method. By default, the response lists the last 500 notebooks. You can choose
305: to paginate the responses with the pageSize query parameter.
306: REST
307: curl -X GET \
308: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
309: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
310: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks:listRecentlyViewed"
311: Replace the following:
312: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
313: values:
314: us for the US multi-region
315: eu for the EU multi-region
316: global for the Global location
317: For more information, see
318: Specify a multi-region
319: for your data store.
320: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
321: LOCATION:
322: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
323: For more information, see Locations.
324: If the request is successful, you should get a JSON response similar to the
325: following. The response contains up to last 500 notebooks that a user
326: accessed recently.
327: {
328: "notebooks": [
329: {
330: "title": "NOTEBOOK_TITLE_1",
331: "notebookId": "NOTEBOOK_ID_1",
332: "emoji": "",
333: "metadata": {
334: "userRole": "PROJECT_ROLE_OWNER",
335: "isShared": false,
336: "isShareable": true,
337: "lastViewed": "LAST_VIEWED_TIME",
338: "createTime": "LAST_CREATED_TIME"
339: },
340: "name": "NOTEBOOK_NAME_1"
341: },
342: {
343: "title": "NOTEBOOK_TITLE_2",
344: "notebookId": "NOTEBOOK_ID_2",
345: "emoji": "",
346: "metadata": {
347: "userRole": "PROJECT_ROLE_OWNER",
348: "isShared": false,
349: "isShareable": true,
350: "lastViewed": "LAST_VIEWED_TIME",
351: "createTime": "LAST_CREATED_TIME"
352: },
353: "name": "NOTEBOOK_NAME_2"
354: }
355: ]
356: }
357: Delete a notebook
358: To delete a notebook, use the
359: notebooks.batchDelete
360: method.
361: REST
362: curl -X POST \
363: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
364: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
365: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks:batchDelete" \
366: -d '{
367: "names": [
368: "NOTEBOOK_NAME"
369: ]
370: }'
371: Replace the following:
372: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
373: values:
374: us for the US multi-region
375: eu for the EU multi-region
376: global for the Global location
377: For more information, see
378: Specify a multi-region
379: for your data store.
380: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
381: LOCATION:
382: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
383: For more information, see Locations.
384: NOTEBOOK_NAME: the complete resource name of the
385: notebook to be deleted. This field has the pattern:
386: projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID.
387: If the request is successful, you receive an empty JSON object. If the
388: notebook doesn't exist, you also receive an empty JSON object, so make
389: sure to specify the notebook name correctly.
390: Share a notebook
391: To share a new notebook, use the
392: notebooks.share
393: method.
394: The user with whom you want to share the notebook must be granted the
395: Cloud NotebookLM User role.
396: REST
397: In your Google Cloud project, assign the Cloud NotebookLM User
398: Identity and Access Management (IAM) role to the users with whom you want to share the
399: notebook.
400: Call the following method.
401: curl -X POST \
402: -H "Authorization:Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
403: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
404: "https://ENDPOINT_LOCATION-discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/notebooks/NOTEBOOK_ID:share" \
405: -d '{
406: "accountAndRoles": [
407: {
408: "email":"USER_EMAIL_1",
409: "role":"USER_ROLE_1",
410: },
411: {
412: "email":"USER_EMAIL_2",
413: "role":"USER_ROLE_2",
414: },
415: ]
416: }'
417: Replace the following:
418: ENDPOINT_LOCATION: the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following
419: values:
420: us for the US multi-region
421: eu for the EU multi-region
422: global for the Global location
423: For more information, see
424: Specify a multi-region
425: for your data store.
426: PROJECT_NUMBER: the number of your Google Cloud project.
427: LOCATION:
428: the geographic location of your data store, such as global.
429: For more information, see Locations.
430: NOTEBOOK_ID: a unique ID to identify
431: the notebook that you want to share. You need the notebook ID for other notebook management
432: tasks, such as sharing or retrieving.
433: USER_EMAIL: the email address of the user with whom
434: you want to share the notebook.
435: USER_ROLE: a role that you want to assign to
436: the user. It can be one of the following:
437: PROJECT_ROLE_WRITER: The user has write permissions on the project.
438: PROJECT_ROLE_READER: The user has read permissions on the project.
439: PROJECT_ROLE_NOT_SHARED:The user has no access to the project.
440: If the request is successful, you receive an empty JSON object.
441: Note: You can't assign PROJECT_ROLE_OWNER with this method. The
442: account that creates a notebook is its owner, and ownership can't be
443: transferred.
444: Verify users using a browser
445: To verify whether you've shared the notebook with the correct users and
446: assigned them correct roles, do the following:
447: Open the notebook in your browser. A notebook has the following URL pattern:
448: If you're using a Google identity:
449: https://notebook.cloud.google.com/LOCATION/notebook/NOTEBOOK_ID?project=PROJECT_NUMBER
450: If you're using a third-party identity:
451: https://notebook.cloud.google/LOCATION/notebook/NOTEBOOK_ID?project=PROJECT_NUMBER
452: Click Share.
453: Verify the users listed as People with access and their assigned roles.

42: The Gemini Notebook API uses OAuth 2.0 to
43: authenticate requests on behalf of a Google user. Every request must include an
44: OAuth 2.0 Bearer token in the Authorization HTTP header. The API doesn't
45: accept API keys.
46: Before you begin
47: Create or select a Google Cloud project. You enable the API, configure
48: the OAuth consent screen, and create OAuth clients in this project. To
49: create a project, see
50: Create a Google Cloud project.
51: Use a personal Google Account. During the Public Preview, the Gemini
52: Notebook API is only available for personal Google Accounts. Requests
53: authenticated with a Google Workspace account fail with
54: 403 PERMISSION_DENIED (WORKSPACE_ACCOUNT_NOT_SUPPORTED).
55: Sign in to Gemini Notebook once. The API reads and writes the notebooks
56: of the authorizing user, so each Google Account must have signed in to
57: Gemini Notebook at least once before calling
58: the API. If an account has never signed in to Gemini Notebook,
59: CreateNotebook requests fail with 404 NOT_FOUND
60: (Account not found for user.).
61: OAuth 2.0 scopes
62: Requests must be authenticated with an OAuth 2.0 token granted one of the
63: following scopes:
64: Scope
65: Access
66: Supported methods
67: https://www.googleapis.com/auth/notebook
68: Read and write access to notebooks and sources
69: CreateNotebook, GetNotebook, ListNotebooks, UpdateNotebook, CreateSource, UploadSource, GetSource, ListSources
70: https://www.googleapis.com/auth/notebook.readonly
71: Read-only access to notebooks and sources
72: GetNotebook, ListNotebooks, GetSource, ListSources
73: Set up OAuth 2.0 for your application
74: To integrate the Gemini Notebook API into a web, desktop, or production
75: application, follow the steps in
76: Using OAuth 2.0 to Access Google APIs to create an
77: OAuth 2.0 client ID in your Google Cloud project:
78: Enable the API: In the
79: Google Cloud Console,
80: select your Google Cloud project and enable the Gemini Notebook API
81: (notebook.googleapis.com).
82: Configure the OAuth consent screen: Go to the
83: Google Auth Platform branding page
84: to configure your app details, and add the
85: https://www.googleapis.com/auth/notebook scope on the
86: Data Access page.
87: Create an OAuth 2.0 client ID: Go to the
88: Clients page, click
89: Create client, and select your application type (for example,
90: Desktop app or Web application). Download the client configuration
91: JSON file as client_secret.json.
92: Request an access token and call the API: Follow the
93: OAuth 2.0 flow for your application
94: type to obtain an access token and pass it in the Authorization: Bearer
95: header:
96: Python
97: from google_auth_oauthlib.flow import InstalledAppFlow
98: import requests
99: SCOPES = ["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/notebook"]
100: flow = InstalledAppFlow.from_client_secrets_file("client_secret.json", SCOPES)
101: creds = flow.run_local_server(port=0)
102: resp = requests.get(
103: "https://notebook.googleapis.com/v1/notebooks",
104: headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {creds.token}"},
105: )
106: print(resp.json())
107: REST
108: curl -s -X GET "https://notebook.googleapis.com/v1/notebooks" \
109: -H "Authorization: Bearer $OAUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN"
110: JavaScript

118: applications, see

121: If you want to try the REST API in your local development environment without
122: creating an OAuth 2.0 client ID first, you can use
123: Application Default Credentials (ADC)
124: with the gcloud CLI.
125: Tip: Want your AI coding assistant to handle Google Cloud project setup and
126: local authentication for you? Copy the setup prompt from the
127: Quickstart or
128: MCP guide.
129: 1. Generate a local token with the gcloud CLI
130: Enable the API in your Google Cloud project and sign in with
131: gcloud auth application-default login:
132: export PROJECT_ID="YOUR_PROJECT_ID"
133: # Enable the Gemini Notebook API in your Google Cloud project
134: gcloud services enable notebook.googleapis.com --project="$PROJECT_ID"
135: # Authenticate with Application Default Credentials and the Gemini Notebook API scope
136: gcloud auth application-default login \
137: --scopes="https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/notebook"
138: # Print an access token for local testing
139: export ACCESS_TOKEN=$(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)
140: 2. Make a request in your local environment
141: When calling the API with a token generated by
142: gcloud auth application-default, pass two headers in your request:
143: Authorization: The Bearer token from
144: gcloud auth application-default print-access-token.
145: x-goog-user-project: The ID of your Google Cloud project that has
146: notebook.googleapis.com enabled (used as the
147: quota project for the
148: request).
149: REST
150: curl -s -X GET "https://notebook.googleapis.com/v1/notebooks" \
151: -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
152: -H "x-goog-user-project: $PROJECT_ID"

155: import requests
156: headers = {
157: "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['ACCESS_TOKEN']}",

159: "Content-Type": "application/json",
160: }
161: resp = requests.get("https://notebook.googleapis.com/v1/notebooks", headers=headers)
162: print(resp.json())

168: "Content-Type": "application/json",
169: },

10: - [Get summary](https://developers.fathom.ai/api-reference/recordings/get-summary.md): This endpoint has two behaviors depending on your request payload: - If you send `destination_url`, the endpoint will behave in an asynchronous manner. - If you do not send `destination_url`, the endpoint will return the data directly.
11: - [Get transcript](https://developers.fathom.ai/api-reference/recordings/get-transcript.md): This endpoint has two behaviors depending on your request payload: - If you send `destination_url`, the endpoint will behave in an asynchronous manner. - If you do not send `destination_url`, the endpoint will return the data directly.
12: - [Request a download](https://developers.fathom.ai/api-reference/recordings/request-a-download.md): Starts async generation of a downloadable file and returns a `download_id` to poll. Video is generated in the background; audio-only recordings complete immediately, so the response may already return `status: completed` with the file payload.
13: - [Get download status](https://developers.fathom.ai/api-reference/recordings/get-download-status.md): Returns the status of a download created with the request-a-download endpoint. When the download is completed, the payload carries a short-lived signed URL for the generated file. Only the API client that created the download can read it.

1: The Consensus API | The Consensus Help Center
2: Skip to main content
3: Back to SearchWebsitePricing
4: Back to SearchWebsitePricing
5: Search for articles...
6: All Collections
7: Explore features
8: The Consensus API
9: The Consensus API
10: Written by Allison Elechko
11: October 12, 2026
12: Table of contents
13: The Consensus API lets you integrate Consensus search directly into your own applications, tools, and workflows. Use it to programmatically search academic research and retrieve relevant papers without needing to run each search manually in Consensus.
14: API access is available directly from your Consensus account. Your API usage and Consensus MCP usage share the same monthly pool of calls. The number of calls included each month depends on your subscription tier.
15: For full technical documentation, endpoints, parameters, and response details, read our API docs here.
16: How to create an API key
17: You can create and manage API keys from the API & MCP Dashboard.
18: Click your profile icon (bottom-left corner)
19: Select API & MCP Dashboard
20: Open the 'Keys and Clients' tab
21: Click 'New key'
22: Give your API key a name so you can identify what you're using it for
23: Create the key and copy it somewhere secure
24: Your full API key is only shown once. Make sure you copy it when you create it.
25: If you lose an API key, you won't be able to view it again. Instead, revoke the existing key and create a new one.
26: Make your first API request
27: Once you've created an API key, you can use it to authenticate requests to the Consensus API.
28: To make a search request, you'll need three things:
29: The Consensus search endpoint: https://api.consensus.app/v1/search
30: Your API key, passed in the x-api-key request header
31: A query parameter containing what you want to search for
32: For example, if you want to search for research on whether creatine improves muscle strength, your request would send that question as the query to the Consensus search endpoint.
33: If you're using a tool such as Postman, a programming language, or another application to make the request, add your Consensus API key as an x-api-key header.
34: The API also supports filters that can help narrow your research, including publication date, study type, sample size, citation count, journal, academic field, country, open-access status, and more.
35: For request examples and a full list of available parameters and responses, see the Consensus API Reference.
36: Use the API to create and manage Threads
37: In addition to standard paper search, the Consensus API can create and manage Threads.
38: Threads are useful for more in-depth research tasks that require multi-step analysis, synthesis, and follow-up questions. Instead of only retrieving a list of papers, a Thread can generate a cited research answer with supporting papers and passages.
39: With the Threads API, you can:
40: Start a new Thread
41: Poll a Thread until the response is ready
42: Add a follow-up question to an existing Thread
43: List historical Threads from your Consensus account
44: Threads created through the API will also appear in your Consensus account. You can open them later in Consensus and continue working with them in the main interface.
45: Thread usage is variable and counts toward your monthly API/MCP usage. A standard paper search typically uses fewer calls, while Threads may use more depending on the research mode, number of papers, and amount of work required.
46: For implementation details and endpoint examples, see the Threads API documentation: https://docs.consensus.app/api-quickstart-threads
47: Search and retrieve full text
48: Consensus can use available full text, not just titles and abstracts, to help retrieve relevant papers.
49: Paid users can also add include_full_text_chunks=true to a search request to return relevant passages from eligible open-access papers:
50: Up to 3 passages per paper
51: Up to 60 passages per request
52: Each passage includes the section of the paper it came from
53: If no eligible passage is available, full_text_chunks returns null
54: Full-text retrieval is used when available on all plans. Returning full-text excerpts is available on Pro, Deep, Teams, and Enterprise plans.
55: For request examples, full-text details, filters, and all available parameters, see the Consensus API documentation.
56: How calls are counted
57: API searches return up to 20 papers by default. You can use the page_size parameter to request more papers per page.
58: Each call covers up to 100 papers:
59: 1-100 papers = 1 call
60: 101-200 papers = 2 calls
61: 201-300 papers = 3 calls
62: And so on, with each additional 100 papers counting as another call
63: More advanced actions, such as creating a Consensus Thread, running a Pro or Deep Thread, or adding follow-up questions to a Thread, may use more calls depending on the amount of work required.
64: Thread usage is variable because Consensus may run multiple research steps, search across more papers, read and synthesize results, and generate a cited response.
65: You can view your usage from your profile > API & MCP Dashboard. The Usage tab shows activity by platform and tool, including searches, created Threads, Pro Threads, and Deep Threads.
66: API and MCP usage limits
67: API and MCP usage share one monthly pool of calls.
68: Plan
69: Included calls per month
70: Maximum calls with additional usage ($0.05/call)
71: Free
72: 30
73: 30 (no additional usage)
74: Pro
75: 500
76: 1,000
77: Team
78: 500
79: 1,000
80: Enterprise
81: 500
82: 1,000
83: Deep
84: 2,000
85: 10,000
86: Additional usage costs $0.05 per call after you've used the calls included in your plan.
87: Your usage resets on the 1st of each month.
88: How to view your API and MCP usage
89: To see your current usage:
90: Click your profile icon in the bottom-left corner
91: Select API & MCP Dashboard
92: At the top of the dashboard, you'll see:
93: Your current usage
94: Any amount due for additional usage
95: Your current plan and reset date
96: The usage bar shows both the number of calls included in your plan and your total monthly call limit.
97: The usage graph shows how your calls are split between API and MCP. You can view your usage for the last 7 days, last 30 days, or your current billing period.
98: How to manage your API keys and MCP clients
99: The Keys and Clients tab is where you manage both your API keys and MCP connections.
100: API keys: you can create and revoke API keys
101: MCP clients: you can connect Consensus to supported clients such as ChatGPT or Claude. If you've already connected a client, you'll see it here.
102: How to enable additional usage
103: Additional usage lets paid users continue making API and MCP calls after using all of the calls included in their plan.
104: Additional usage is turned off by default.
105: To enable it:
106: Open the API & MCP Dashboard
107: Select the settings control in the upper-right corner
108: Under API & MCP settings, turn on Enable additional usage
109: Save your changes
110: Once enabled, calls beyond your plan's included amount are billed at $0.05 per call, up to your plan's maximum monthly call limit.
111: You can turn additional usage off at any time. If you turn it off after you've already exceeded your included calls, you won't be able to make any more API or MCP calls until your usage resets. You'll still be billed for any additional calls made before you turned additional usage off.
112: Free users cannot enable additional usage. To access additional usage, upgrade to a paid plan.
113: Common API errors
114: API Error message
115: Cause
116: Fix
117: 401 - Invalid authentication credentials
118: The API key is incorrect, revoked, or isn't being sent using the required header.
119: Confirm you're using the correct API key in the x-api-key header. If you've lost the key, revoke it in the API & MCP Dashboard and create a new one.
120: 402 - Billing past due
121: Your subscription is past due, usually because a payment failed. API and MCP calls are paused until the billing issue is resolved.
122: Update your payment method and resolve the outstanding payment to restore access.
123: 429 - You've used all included {30, 500, 2,000, etc.} searches this month. Resets on {date}.
124: You've used all of the API/MCP calls included in your plan.
125: Paid users can enable additional usage from the API & MCP Dashboard, if they haven't reached their plan's maximum monthly call limit. Otherwise, wait until the reset date shown in the error message.
126: 429 - Too many requests
127: Requests are being sent faster than the current rate limit of one request per second.
128: Slow down your requests and try again.
129: Keep your API key secure
130: Treat your API key like a password.
131: Don't share it publicly or include it in publicly accessible client-side code, public repositories, screenshots, or other places where someone else could access it.
132: If you believe a key has been exposed, revoke it from the API & MCP Dashboard and create a new one.
133: You can manage your API keys, monitor API and MCP usage, review billing, and change your additional usage settings at any time from the API & MCP Dashboard.
134: FAQs
135: Where can I see my API/MCP billing history?
136: Go to the API & MCP Dashboard, then click the Billing History tab.
137: Do API and MCP have separate usage limits?
138: No, your monthly usage limit is shared across API and MCP.
139: What happens if I lose my API key?
140: You won't be able to view the key again. Revoke the lost key and create a new one from the 'Keys and Clients' tab.

74: A short, video-first guide to Consensus for researchers at any level. Learn to search, read, and organise the literature on your topic, one lesson at a time.
75: Copy pageCopy page
76: Consensus is an AI search engine for research. You ask a question, it searches over 400 million scholarly articles, including 350 million peer-reviewed research papers, and it writes an answer where every sentence links back to the paper it came from.
77: It’s a search engine first. It finds the papers, then uses AI to read and summarize them. It doesn’t make things up from general knowledge, so you can always click through and check the source.
78: How this guide works
79: This guide is for researchers at any level, whether you’re starting your first project or you’ve been publishing for years. Each lesson is a short video plus a prompt to try on your own topic. Start at the top if you’re new to Consensus, or jump straight to the task you need.

90: Key features
91: Reference pages for search, Research Agent, Deep Review, Library, and more.
92: All the videos are also in one YouTube playlist.
93: New to research terms like “meta-analysis” or “preprint”? Keep Research terms in plain English open in another tab.
94: Where you can use Consensus
95: Web app
96: Everything in this guide happens at consensus.app. It’s free to start.
97: In ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, or the API
98: Connect Consensus to the AI assistant you already use in one click, or build on it with the API.
99: Why researchers trust Consensus
100: Search happens before AI. The AI only summarizes papers Consensus actually found. If nothing relevant turns up, it tells you.
101: Every claim is checkable. Hover a citation to see the exact quote from the paper. See Check a claim against the paper.
102: Retracted papers are flagged and never used in answers.
103: Your data isn’t training data. Consensus doesn’t train models on your searches or uploads.
104: It’s measured. In blinded evaluations judged by PhD researchers, Consensus finds more relevant papers than Google Scholar and than frontier models with web search. See Benchmarks.
105: More relevant than Google Scholar
106: 88.1% vs 81.8% precision on 500 real user queries, judged blind by PhD researchers.
107: Beats GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8, 10x faster
108: More relevant top-20 papers at a median of 8.7 seconds, versus 75 to 103 seconds.
109: AI is a research assistant, not a replacement for reading. Use it to find and understand papers faster, then read the ones that matter.

1: # Consensus
2: > Developer documentation for Consensus, the AI research engine.
3: - [Start here](https://docs.consensus.app/get-started/what-is-consensus.md): A short, video-first guide to Consensus for researchers at any level. Learn to search, read, and organise the literature on your topic, one lesson at a time.
4: - [Run your first search](https://docs.consensus.app/get-started/run-your-first-search.md): Type a research question, pick what to search, and read what comes back. Keyword searches and full questions both work.
5: - [Where the papers come from](https://docs.consensus.app/get-started/where-papers-come-from.md): Consensus has the second-largest research index in the world: abstracts and metadata for 400 million scholarly articles, including 350 million peer-reviewed research papers, open-access full text, and paywalled full text through publisher partnerships, updated weekly.
6: - [Read the full paper](https://docs.consensus.app/get-started/full-text-access.md): Consensus reads the whole paper, not just the abstract, including paywalled articles from major publishers, open-access PDFs, and papers you upload yourself.
7: - [Go deeper with Deep Review](https://docs.consensus.app/get-started/deep-review.md): A Deep Review runs many searches, reads 50 to 100 papers, and writes a longer report. Use it when one search isn't enough to answer your question.
8: - [Save papers to your Library](https://docs.consensus.app/get-started/save-papers-to-your-library.md): Bookmark papers and searches as you go, and keep them in a Collection for your project so nothing gets lost.
9: - [Use Consensus in ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, or with the API](https://docs.consensus.app/core-features/mcp.md): Connect Consensus to ChatGPT, Claude, or Microsoft 365 Copilot in one click, or build on it with the API, so answers cite real peer-reviewed papers.
10: - [Read a thread](https://docs.consensus.app/learn/read-a-consensus-answer.md): What every part of a search result means: the search trace, the written answer, the citations, and the reference list with its study types and citation counts.
11: - [Check a claim](https://docs.consensus.app/core-features/citation-grounding.md): Citation Grounding shows the exact quote behind every citation in a Consensus answer. Hover to see the passage, click to jump to it in the paper.
12: - [Ask a paper](https://docs.consensus.app/learn/ask-questions-about-a-paper.md): Attach a paper to the search bar and ask about its methods, sample, findings, and limitations, so you understand a study before you cite it.
13: - [Filter for recent studies](https://docs.consensus.app/search-basics/find-high-quality-recent-papers.md): Cut through preprints and low-impact work. Stack year, journal quality, and citation filters in plain language, then visualize the results on a research timeline.
14: - [Find popular papers](https://docs.consensus.app/search-basics/find-seminal-papers.md): New to a field? Surface the foundational papers, deep-read the most cited one, and map its citation graph in three searches.
15: - [Research terms dictionary](https://docs.consensus.app/learn/research-terms.md): A short glossary of the research words you'll see in Consensus and in papers, from corpus and preprint to meta-analysis and effect size.
16: - [See how the field got here](https://docs.consensus.app/search-basics/map-field-history.md): Get the historical arc of a field, not just a list of papers. Early foundations, key breakthroughs, and what changed in the last three years.
17: - [Spot the main findings and themes](https://docs.consensus.app/learn/spot-main-findings.md): Group the research on your topic into themes, rank them by how strong the evidence is, and put the main findings into your own words.
18: - [Compare studies side by side](https://docs.consensus.app/search-basics/build-a-comparison-table.md): Compare interventions side by side with the same metrics. Run parallel searches, then extract sample size, session count, follow-up duration, and effect size into one table.
19: - [Find where studies disagree](https://docs.consensus.app/learn/where-studies-disagree.md): Find the questions your field hasn't settled, understand why studies reach different results, and spot the limitations that matter.
20: - [Follow a paper's citations](https://docs.consensus.app/search-basics/trace-citations.md): Understand where a paper came from and how the field built on it. Bi-directional citation tracing using Attention Is All You Need as the anchor.
21: - [Grow a reading list from a paper](https://docs.consensus.app/search-basics/snowball-reading-list.md): Start from one paper you trust and triangulate similarity, citations, and references to find every adjacent study, then map the gaps.
22: - [Explore the citation graph](https://docs.consensus.app/learn/explore-the-citation-graph.md): See how papers connect through citations on a visual map. Start from a paper you trust and find the work it built on and the work that followed.
23: - [Look up a researcher's work](https://docs.consensus.app/search-basics/research-an-author.md): Map a researcher's publications, find their most influential paper, and trace its downstream impact. Useful before a meeting, a hire, or a citation.
24: - [Build Collections for your project](https://docs.consensus.app/learn/build-collections.md): Organise your project's papers into Collections by theme, add papers from anywhere, ask questions of everything you've saved, and share it with collaborators.
25: - [Find research gaps](https://docs.consensus.app/learn/find-research-gaps.md): Ask Consensus what's missing from the papers you've saved, such as populations, study types, or topics, then search the full index for papers that fill those gaps.
26: - [Add your own PDFs](https://docs.consensus.app/search-basics/private-documents.md): Upload internal reports, proprietary data, or unpublished documents into a Collection and search them alongside 400M+ scholarly articles, privately.
27: - [Connect two fields](https://docs.consensus.app/search-basics/bridge-two-fields.md): Bridge two disciplines in one thread: establish the limits in your field, find where they show up in another, map the gaps, and find collaborators.
28: - [Check a manuscript's citations](https://docs.consensus.app/search-basics/manuscript-citation-check.md): Upload your manuscript and use a Deep Review to find supporting and challenging studies, surface papers you missed, and do a final gut check before submitting.
29: - [Review a grant before you submit](https://docs.consensus.app/search-basics/grant-review.md): Upload your grant and use a Deep Review to find similar studies, compare designs, identify literature gaps, and validate your effect size and sample size assumptions.
30: - [Catch up on a fast-moving field](https://docs.consensus.app/search-basics/catch-up-on-a-field.md): Fifty new papers a week and no time to read them. Build a what's-new-and-what's-strongest digest grouped by approach, then drill into the winning papers.
31: - [Paper search](https://docs.consensus.app/get-started/how-search-works.md): Consensus finds the most relevant papers with hybrid keyword and semantic search, ranks them the way a researcher would weigh them, refines the top 20 with a larger model, and only then uses AI to synthesize an answer.
32: - [How Consensus compares](https://docs.consensus.app/benchmarks.md): Blinded evaluations of Consensus search on real user queries: more relevant papers than Google Scholar (88.1% vs 81.8% precision), and more relevant than GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 with web search at a median of 8.7 seconds versus 75 to 103 seconds.
33: - [Research Agent](https://docs.consensus.app/core-features/research-agent.md): Research Agent is the AI research assistant behind every Pro message and Deep Review in Consensus. It plans searches, chains tools, applies academic filters, and returns citation-backed answers.
34: - [Deep Review](https://docs.consensus.app/core-features/deep-search.md): Deep is a longer, more robust version of a Consensus search. It runs up to 20 searches in parallel, uses multiple Research Agent tools like citation crawl, and reads 50 to 100 papers before answering.
35: - [Library](https://docs.consensus.app/core-features/library.md): My Library is where you save, organize, and work with research in Consensus. Store papers, searches, and uploaded documents in Collections, import from Zotero, and chat with everything you've collected.
36: - [Citation Graph](https://docs.consensus.app/core-features/citation-graph.md): Citation Graph is a visual way to explore how papers connect. Start with up to 5 seed papers you trust and discover related work through citation relationships instead of keywords.
37: - [Skills](https://docs.consensus.app/core-features/skills.md): Skills are ready-made research workflows built into the Consensus search bar. Pick one, such as Literature Review or Verify Citations, and Consensus runs the whole task for you as a Deep Review.
38: - [Extract data](https://docs.consensus.app/core-features/extract-data.md): Extract data turns a set of papers into a table that Consensus fills in for you. Each paper is a row, each column is a question, and every answer links to the quote it came from.
39: - [Get started with Consensus API](https://docs.consensus.app/api-get-started.md): Search over 400 million scholarly articles, including 350 million peer-reviewed research papers, with the Consensus REST API.
40: - [Full text in the API](https://docs.consensus.app/api-full-text.md): Read inside papers with the Consensus API: query-matched excerpts from open-access papers in every paid search, and the complete text of open-access papers as Markdown.
41: - [API plans and access](https://docs.consensus.app/api-plans-and-access.md): What each Consensus plan includes on the API: monthly calls, papers per request, pagination, full-text excerpts, complete text, citations, and rate limits.
42: - [Consensus API compared with PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar](https://docs.consensus.app/api-comparison.md): Why teams build on the Consensus API, how it works alongside PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Crossref, and how the APIs compare on coverage, search, evidence metadata, full text, pricing and rate limits.
43: - [Biomedical search: Consensus, PubMed and Europe PMC](https://docs.consensus.app/api-comparison/pubmed-europe-pmc.md): How the Consensus API compares with PubMed E-utilities and the Europe PMC REST API for biomedical literature search: semantic search, study-design filters, clinical guidelines, full text, and when a Boolean strategy is the right tool.
44: - [Open metadata APIs: Consensus, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Crossref](https://docs.consensus.app/api-comparison/openalex-semantic-scholar-crossref.md): How the Consensus API compares with OpenAlex, the Semantic Scholar API and the Crossref REST API: coverage, semantic search, evidence metadata, licences, and how to enrich Consensus results with open metadata.
45: - [Retrieval for RAG and AI agents](https://docs.consensus.app/api-comparison/rag-and-ai-agents.md): What a RAG pipeline or research agent needs from a scholarly search API, how Consensus compares with PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar for grounding, and when web search APIs like Exa and Tavily fit.
46: - [Pricing, rate limits and data privacy](https://docs.consensus.app/api-comparison/pricing-and-privacy.md): Pricing, rate limits, interfaces and data use compared across the Consensus API, PubMed E-utilities, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Crossref, including what each provider does with your queries.
47: - [Search quality evaluations](https://docs.consensus.app/api-comparison/evaluations.md): Two blind relevance evaluations of Consensus search: against Google Scholar on 500 real queries, and against GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 with web search on 100 real queries. Methods, results and caveats.
48: - [What you can build with the Consensus API](https://docs.consensus.app/api-use-cases.md)

87: - [Microsoft Copilot Studio](https://docs.consensus.app/enterprise/copilot-studio.md): Add the Consensus MCP server as a Model Context Protocol tool in Copilot Studio, with per-user OAuth or a shared API key, so your own agents can search 400 million papers.
88: - [AI gateways and MCP registries](https://docs.consensus.app/enterprise/gateways/overview.md): Register the Consensus MCP server in the gateway your organization already runs. The same five facts work everywhere; product pages give the exact field names.
89: - [TrueFoundry AI Gateway](https://docs.consensus.app/enterprise/gateways/truefoundry.md): Register the Consensus MCP server in TrueFoundry's MCP Gateway with a shared API key or per-user OAuth.
90: - [LiteLLM MCP Gateway](https://docs.consensus.app/enterprise/gateways/litellm.md): Add the Consensus MCP server to LiteLLM's config.yaml with a bearer token or per-user OAuth with Dynamic Client Registration.
91: - [Cloudflare MCP Server Portals](https://docs.consensus.app/enterprise/gateways/cloudflare.md): Add the Consensus MCP server to a Cloudflare One MCP Portal so users reach it through one Access-protected URL.
92: - [IBM ContextForge MCP Gateway](https://docs.consensus.app/enterprise/gateways/ibm-contextforge.md): Register the Consensus MCP server in IBM's open-source ContextForge gateway with a bearer token or per-user OAuth.
93: - [Azure API Management](https://docs.consensus.app/enterprise/gateways/azure-api-management.md): Expose the Consensus MCP server through Azure API Management as a passthrough MCP server, with a bearer token injected by policy.
94: - [AWS Bedrock AgentCore Gateway](https://docs.consensus.app/enterprise/gateways/aws-agentcore.md): Add the Consensus MCP server as an MCP target in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with an API key credential provider.
95: - [Portkey MCP Gateway](https://docs.consensus.app/enterprise/gateways/portkey.md): Register the Consensus MCP server in Portkey's MCP Registry with custom headers or per-user OAuth.
96: - [Obot MCP Gateway](https://docs.consensus.app/enterprise/gateways/obot.md): Add the Consensus MCP server to Obot as a remote server with custom headers or spec-compliant per-user OAuth.
97: - [Other gateways](https://docs.consensus.app/enterprise/gateways/other-gateways.md): Kong, Solo.io agentgateway, Zuplo, Docker MCP Gateway, and Boomi AI Gateway can front the Consensus MCP server with a static bearer header; each has a caveat worth knowing.
98: - [What you can build with the Consensus API and MCP](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases.md): Search 400+ million research papers and read the full text of open-access ones, for internal tools, scientific agents, and custom research systems.
99: - [Start building with the Consensus API and MCP](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/get-started.md): Pick a surface, run your first filtered search, and find the guide for what you are building.
100: - [Best practices](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/best-practices.md): The five primitives every Consensus workflow is built from, and how to tell a good use case from a poor one before you build it.
101: - [Build internal research tools](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/internal-tools.md): How enterprise R&D teams, biotechs, and AI startups connect Consensus paper search to internal assistants, monitoring agents, literature tables, and scientific agents.
102: - [Build custom research systems](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/research-systems.md): How academics and research groups use the Consensus API and MCP to build literature-review, writing, and reporting workflows they can reproduce.
103: - [Use case library](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/gallery.md): Worked examples of what people build on Consensus, filterable by persona, each with the full prompt and API call behind it.
104: - [Find a real citation for every claim in a draft](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/ground-a-manuscript.md): Paste a draft section and get every empirical claim matched to a real, verifiable paper — or flagged as unsupported before a reviewer finds it.
105: - [Verify that every citation is real and supports its claim](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/citation-verification.md): Verify every reference in a document actually exists, then confirm each one says what the text citing it claims.
106: - [Turn a syllabus into a recommended reading list](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/syllabus-reading-list.md): Extract course topics and learning outcomes from a syllabus, then produce a curated reading list of recent research with summaries and discussion questions.
107: - [Build and maintain a Library collection from your assistant](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/library-reading-list.md): Have the Consensus research agent find papers, save them into a Library collection, then audit, filter, and rename that collection over MCP or the API.
108: - [Find NIH grants for a research idea](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/grant-finder.md): Position a research idea against the literature, map it to the right NIH institutes and study sections, and surface NOSIs, open FOAs, and funded overlap.
109: - [Screen abstracts against inclusion criteria](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/abstract-screening.md): Apply explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria across thousands of abstracts, with a decision log a second reviewer can audit.
110: - [Build a PRISMA-ready search corpus](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/prisma-corpus.md): Assemble a reproducible, deduplicated record set with the flow counts a systematic review has to report.
111: - [Write the search-strategy section of your methods](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/search-strategy-methods.md): Turn a logged search into the reproducible methods paragraph reviewers ask for — accurate because it was recorded as it ran.
112: - [Find which journals to submit to](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/where-to-submit.md): Identify the journals actually publishing work like yours, with their quartile, so you target a realistic venue first.
113: - [Track how a field's terminology changed over time](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/terminology-shift.md): Compare old and recent literature on the same concept so you search the terms the field actually used, not just the ones it uses now.
114: - [Create a biomarker evidence report](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/biomarker-report.md): Assess the evidence for a biomarker's optimal range across Mendelian randomization, large cohorts, and trials — or establish that no evidence-based range exists.
115: - [Build a drug target validation dossier](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/target-evidence-tiers.md): Human genetics, in vitro, animal, and clinical evidence for one target in a single pass — including what contradicts it.
116: - [Monitor new research about a drug, device, or brand](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/brand-and-device-monitoring.md): Track what gets published about a drug, device, or brand, and route only the papers that change something.
117: - [Grade a set of papers with your own evidence rubric](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/evidence-grading-rubric.md): Apply your organization's standard for what counts as good evidence, consistently, across every paper on a topic.
118: - [Find the leading investigators in an indication](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/investigator-mapping.md): Rank the authors publishing most in a therapeutic area, split by region and by recent versus lifetime output.
119: - [Assemble a payer evidence dossier](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/payer-evidence-dossier.md): Pull the cost-effectiveness, burden-of-illness, and real-world evidence a reimbursement submission needs, in one pass.
120: - [Check whether a finding has human evidence yet](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/translational-readiness.md): Separate cell and animal work from human studies for a claim, and report the ratio — the number that tells you how translated a finding really is.
121: - [Extract numbers and formulas from full-text papers](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/extract-values-from-full-text.md): Pull numbers, formulas, and parameters out of papers with their measurement conditions attached.
122: - [Substantiate a product claim with published evidence](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/claim-substantiation.md): Build the evidence file behind a claim before it ships — including what contradicts it.
123: - [Compare candidate materials against published test data](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/materials-comparison.md): Search published performance data for each candidate under your actual operating conditions, and find out which combinations nobody has tested.
124: - [Find published work on a failure or degradation mechanism](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/failure-mode-scan.md): Check whether a defect you are seeing is a known mechanism with a published cause, before you spend a quarter rediscovering it.
125: - [Find published process conditions for a manufacturing step](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/process-window-precedent.md): See what temperature, time, atmosphere, and concentration ranges others have published for a process, so you start from precedent rather than from scratch.
126: - [Check a supplier's performance claim against independent research](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/supplier-claim-check.md): Test what a vendor says their material, tool, or process achieves against what the published literature independently reports.
127: - [Find human-factors evidence for a design decision](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/human-factors-evidence.md): Pull the biomechanics, ergonomics, and usability research behind a product or workstation choice, before the decision gets defended after the fact.
128: - [Build a reusable literature-review workflow](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/literature-review-skill.md): A repeatable review workflow that picks a search framework, allocates a search budget, and synthesizes findings into a research guide your whole team can run the same way.
129: - [Track new papers across many topics on a schedule](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/scheduled-research-pipeline.md): Sweep hundreds of topics on a cron, diff against the last run, and report only what changed.
130: - [Swap a hand-maintained paper corpus for full-text search](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/swap-a-paper-corpus.md): Replace a curated PubMed subset you maintain yourself with a weekly-refreshed full-text index, without rebuilding the infrastructure.
131: - [Add a citable evidence layer to an agent you already ship](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/add-an-evidence-layer.md): Give a working agent access to peer-reviewed literature as a tool, so its claims carry citations instead of assertions.
132: - [Answer one question with many parallel searches](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/parallel-search-angles.md): Decompose a research question into multiple search angles, gather evidence across all of them, and distill one cited answer.
133: - [Screen thousands of target-disease pairs for evidence](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/high-throughput-screening.md): Pull literature evidence for every pair in a large matrix — the batch workload that breaks most retrieval APIs.
134: - [Benchmark literature providers against your own ground truth](https://docs.consensus.app/use-cases/benchmark-retrieval.md): Build a curated query set with known-relevant papers and measure which retrieval provider actually surfaces them.

1: # Devin Docs
2: - [Cloud (105 pages)](https://docs.devin.ai/_llms/en/cloud.txt): Get Started, Essential Guidelines, Onboarding Devin, Working with Devin, Product Guides, Integrations, Admin, Release Notes.
3: - [Desktop (96 pages)](https://docs.devin.ai/_llms/en/desktop.txt): Devin Desktop, Agent Command Center, Releases, Windsurf Plugins, Accounts, Security.
4: - [API (315 pages)](https://docs.devin.ai/_llms/en/api.txt): Getting Started, Concepts, Agent Lifecycle, Context Management, Environment Management, Automation, Integrations, Analytics, Observability, Devin for Security, Infrastructure, Identity & Access, Configuration, Legacy API v1, Legacy API v2.
5: ## CLI
6: ### Getting Started
7: - [Quickstart](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/index.md): Get up and running in 2 minutes with Devin CLI, a local command-line coding agent with deep Devin Cloud integration.
8: - [Introducing Devin CLI](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/introducing-devin-cli.md): A two-minute video tour of Devin CLI: start a local coding agent in your terminal, hand work to Devin Cloud, and pick up PRs locally.
9: - [Essential Commands](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/essential-commands.md): The must-know Devin CLI commands: starting and resuming sessions, cloud sessions, slash commands, and keyboard shortcuts.
10: - [Subagents](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/subagents.md): Delegate tasks to independent subagents in the Devin CLI that run in the foreground or background with their own profiles and permissions
11: - [Devin Cloud in the Devin CLI](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/cloud.md): Create, steer, resume, and watch Devin Cloud sessions from your terminal with devin --cloud, /cloud, /open, /model, and /rename.
12: - [SSH into Devin Cloud sessions](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/ssh.md): Connect to a Devin Cloud session's VM over SSH with devin ssh, forward ports with devin forward, and copy files with scp from the Devin CLI.
13: - [Hand off to cloud Devins](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/handoff.md): Hand off a task from the Devin CLI to a cloud Devin session with /handoff, and bring a cloud session's pull request back to your machine.
14: - [Models](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/models.md): Available models in Devin CLI and how to configure them, including Adaptive routing and Fusion pairings.
15: - [Adaptive](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/adaptive.md): Adaptive is Cognition's intelligent model router that automatically selects the best AI model for each task.
16: - [Fusion in Devin CLI](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/fusion.md): Fusion pairs a frontier lead model with a cost-efficient sidekick, delivering frontier intelligence at a lower cost in Devin CLI.
17: - [Sandbox](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/sandbox.md): OS-level isolation for Devin CLI sessions: how the sandbox works, network filtering, and enterprise enforcement.
18: - [Troubleshooting](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/troubleshooting.md): Common issues and how to fix them
19: ### Editor Integrations
20: - [JetBrains](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/acp/jetbrains.md): Run Devin inside JetBrains IDEs from AI Chat using the Agent Client Protocol (ACP), including JetBrains Remote Development.
21: - [Zed](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/acp/zed.md): Run Devin CLI inside the Zed editor as a custom ACP agent in the Agent Panel, including install, authentication, and model selection.
22: - [Xcode](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/acp/xcode.md): Run Devin inside Xcode's coding assistant via the Agent Client Protocol (ACP), or give the Devin CLI access to your Xcode project through Xcode's MCP bridge.
23: ### Extensibility
24: - [Extensibility Overview](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/extensibility/index.md): Customize and extend Devin CLI with rules, skills, plugins, subagents, MCP servers, and hooks, or import configuration from other tools.
25: - [Configuration](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/extensibility/configuration.md): How to configure Devin CLI behavior with config files
26: - [Rules & AGENTS.md](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/extensibility/rules.md): Provide always-on instructions and context that guide the agent in every session
27: - [MCP Overview](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/extensibility/mcp/overview.md): Extend Devin CLI with external tool servers using the Model Context Protocol
28: - [MCP Configuration](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/extensibility/mcp/configuration.md): How to add, configure, authenticate, and troubleshoot MCP servers in Devin CLI, including stdio, Streamable HTTP, and SSE transports.
29: - [Skills Overview](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/extensibility/skills/overview.md): Skills are reusable SKILL.md prompts and workflows for Devin CLI, invoked with a slash command or by the agent, with their own permissions.
30: - [Creating Skills](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/extensibility/skills/creating-skills.md): Full reference for the Devin CLI SKILL.md format: frontmatter options, allowed-tools auto-approval, permissions, and subagent skills.
31: - [Devin CLI plugins](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/extensibility/plugins/overview.md): Install, author, and govern plugins in the Devin CLI: plugin format, devin plugins commands, the manifest, and inheritance levels.
32: - [Quickstart: team marketplace](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/extensibility/plugins/quickstart.md): Set up a shared Devin plugin marketplace for your team with reusable skills, rules, hooks, MCP servers, and governance.
33: - [Hooks](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/extensibility/hooks/overview.md): Configure Devin CLI hooks to run shell commands or LLM prompts on lifecycle events, block or rewrite tool calls, and inject context.
34: - [Lifecycle Hooks](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/extensibility/hooks/lifecycle-hooks.md): Reference for each Devin hook event (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, PostCompaction, SessionStart, SessionEnd): stdin fields and examples.
35: ### Enterprise
36: - [Devin Auth](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/enterprise/devin-auth.md): Authenticate to Devin CLI with your existing Devin account, and use custom roles with the Use Devin CLI permission to control enterprise access.
37: - [Legacy Windsurf Auth](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/enterprise/windsurf-auth.md): Authenticate to Devin CLI with your existing legacy Windsurf Enterprise account, including per-user CLI access requirements and billing.
38: - [Devin CLI Team Settings](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/enterprise/team-settings.md): Configure team-wide Devin CLI settings for your enterprise, including model allowlists, the default model, MCP servers, and web search.
39: - [System Configuration](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/enterprise/system-config.md): Pin Devin CLI login and proxy settings across managed devices with an MDM-distributed system.json policy
40: - [Devin CLI Controls](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/enterprise/controls.md): Enterprise controls for Devin CLI and the Devin Local agent: which legacy Cascade controls carry over, are replaced by permissions, or are unsupported.
41: ### Reference
42: - [Commands & Flags](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/reference/commands.md): Complete Devin CLI reference for global flags, subcommands such as devin auth, mcp, ssh, and forward, and interactive slash commands.
43: - [Keyboard Shortcuts](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/reference/keyboard-shortcuts.md): Learn Devin CLI keyboard shortcuts for composing drafts, cancelling tasks, changing modes, editing text, and rebinding keys.
44: - [Terminal Compatibility](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/reference/terminal-compatibility.md): Devin CLI terminal compatibility: supported terminal emulators, recommendations per platform, and Option-as-Meta setup on macOS.
45: - [Configuration File](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/reference/configuration/config-file.md): Complete reference for the Devin CLI config file format, including every user and project option such as permissions, proxy, sandbox, and read_config_from.
46: - [Configuration Import](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/reference/configuration/read-config-from.md): Control how Devin CLI imports settings from Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Codex, Kiro, OpenCode, and Zed
47: - [Configuration Precedence](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/reference/configuration/global-vs-local.md): How global, project, and local settings interact
48: - [Devin CLI permissions](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/reference/permissions.md): Configure Devin CLI permission rules to allow, deny, or prompt for commands, file access, and MCP tools with predictable precedence.
49: ### Changelog
50: - [Changelog (Stable)](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/changelog/stable.md): Release notes for the Devin CLI stable channel: new features, improvements, and fixes in each stable release of the command-line interface.
51: ## Enterprise
52: ### Getting Started
53: - [Getting Started with Devin Enterprise](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/getting-started/get-started.md): Step-by-step guide for configuring Devin Enterprise, including organizations, user roles, SSO, and integrations.
54: - [Understanding Organizations](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/getting-started/organizations.md): Learn how organizations work in Devin Enterprise and how to map them to your teams, repositories, identity provider groups, and budgets.
55: ### Deployment
56: - [Enterprise Deployment](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/deployment/overview.md): Learn about Devin's enterprise deployment options: Enterprise Cloud and Customer Dedicated Deployment architectures.
57: - [Dedicated Deployment Private Networking](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/deployment/dedicated_saas_private_networking.md): Connect a Devin Dedicated Deployment to internal systems such as GitHub Enterprise Server, GitLab, and Artifactory privately over AWS PrivateLink.
58: - [Devin Connect](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/deployment/devin-connect.md): Devin Connect gives Devin private access to internal systems: deploy a gateway as a policy proxy, reached by an outbound-only tunnel or AWS PrivateLink.
59: ### Environment management
60: - [Enterprise environment overview](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/environment-management/overview.md): Enterprise-wide environment management: blueprint hierarchy, enterprise blueprint configuration, secrets, and enterprise-wide rebuilds.
61: - [Devin environment rollout health](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/environment-management/rollout.md): Use Devin's Enterprise Rollout page to monitor blueprint adoption, build health, and environment readiness across organizations.
62: - [Best practices](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/environment-management/best-practices.md): Enterprise best practices for organizing blueprints, managing secrets, monitoring builds, pinning, and migration at scale.
63: ### Local agent controls
64: - [Local Agent Controls](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/local/controls.md): Configure Devin Desktop and Devin CLI settings across your enterprise with a root-level baseline and per-organization overrides.
65: ### Usage management
66: - [Usage policies: budgets and user limits](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/features/usage-policies.md): Cap ACU usage with budgets for shared pools and user limits for each member, with usage tiers, IdP group mappings, overrides, and usage requests.
67: - [Devin Coach: usage efficiency coaching](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/features/devin-coach.md): Devin Coach flags inefficient prompts in the input box before you send them and gives admins analytics on suggestion outcomes and blockers.
68: ### Integrations
69: - [Git Integrations](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/integrations/git-integrations.md): Connect Devin Enterprise to your source code provider in Settings > Connections and grant organizations access to repositories in Settings > Repositories.
70: - [GitHub Enterprise Server Integration](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/integrations/github-enterprise-server.md): Connect Devin with GitHub Enterprise Server or GitHub Enterprise Cloud with Data Residency
71: - [GitLab Self-Managed Integration](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/integrations/gitlab-self-managed.md): Connect Devin with your self-managed GitLab instance (version 16.6 or later): admin setup, service accounts, webhooks, and user linking.
72: - [Azure DevOps](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/integrations/azure-devops.md): Connect Devin to Azure DevOps with OAuth so Devin can clone repositories, open pull requests, and work within your Azure DevOps organization.
73: - [Azure DevOps (Service Principal)](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/integrations/azure-devops-service-principal.md): Connect Devin to Azure DevOps using a Microsoft Entra service principal, then grant organizations repository access and add repos to environments.
74: - [Artifacts](https://docs.devin.ai/enterprise/integrations/artifacts/overview.md): Connect Devin to JFrog Artifactory, AWS CodeArtifact, and Azure Artifacts by adding artifact credentials and tools to your environment blueprint.
75: ### Security & Access

29: How to Generate AI Video From Your Terminal With Higgsfield CLI
30: Higgsfield
31: 11 min
32: Higgsfield CLI lets you generate images and videos from a terminal, script or coding agent without opening the web app. It installs with curl, Homebrew or npm and runs the same models as the web app from the same account and credit balance. One command creates a generation, another shows its cost first, and --json makes every answer readable for scripts and agents.
33: What Is Higgsfield CLI?
34: This guide covers installation, sign-in, an image and a video made from that image, cost checks, Soul ID, batch scripts and the difference between CLI, MCP and the Higgsfield API. Higgsfield CLI is an open-source command-line client for Higgsfield, an AI-native creative suite for video and image generation. The code and releases are on GitHub. The command is higgsfield, with higgs as a shorter alias.
35: Three things define how it works:
36: No API key. You sign in through the browser with a regular Higgsfield account.
37: Same credits. Every generation is charged to that account's plan credits at standard rates.
38: Web-only access stays on the web. Unlimited model access and free generations do not apply to CLI generations.
39: What Is Higgsfield CLI?
40: Area
41: What the CLI covers
42: Command group
43: Generation
44: 35+ models and tools for image, video, 3D and audio, plus analysis such as Virality Predictor
45: generate, model
46: Characters
47: Training and reusing Soul characters
48: soul-id
49: Workflows
50: Reframe, dubbing, voice change, draw-to-video
51: workflow
52: Account
53: Balance, transactions, billing workspaces
54: account, workspace
55: Beyond generation
56: Marketing Studio assets, product photoshoots, website and game deployment
57: marketing-studio, product-photoshoot, website, game
58: Websites, games and the Video Explainer flow live in the same tool, but this guide stays on image and video. The full command reference is in the README on GitHub.
59: Quick Start: From Install to First Batch
60: The whole path takes six commands. Each step is explained in its own section below.
61: 1. Install with one method. Or use curl (curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/higgsfield-ai/cli/main/install.sh | sh) or npm (npm install -g @higgsfield/cli).
62: brew install higgsfield-ai/tap/higgsfield
63: 2. Check the version.
64: higgsfield version
65: 3. Sign in through the browser.
66: higgsfield auth login
67: 4. Generate one image.
68: higgsfield generate create nano_banana_2 --prompt "1980s flash photo on film: a young man with shaggy dark hair in a black glossy leather jacket with a red flame shape painted on the back, seen from behind, turns his head in profile while talking on a payphone on a subway platform. Silver trains on both sides, the left one blurred as it rushes past, a yellow platform edge, chrome pipes with fluorescent lights overhead. No text, no signs." --aspect_ratio 16:9 --wait --json
69: 5. Check the price, then generate one video from that image.
70: higgsfield generate cost seedance_2_5 --mode omni_reference --start-image <image_job_id> --prompt "Start from the start frame. 1980s film look, handheld, slow push-in. He listens on the payphone, tense. The left train rushes past, the roar drowns the call, he frowns and shouts \"Hello? I can't hear you!\" The train leaves, sudden quiet, he hears the voice, exhales and smiles: \"Yeah... I'm here.\" Train wind moves his hair, window light flickers on his face. No text." --duration 5 --resolution 1080p
71: higgsfield generate create seedance_2_5 --mode omni_reference --start-image <image_job_id> --prompt "Start from the start frame. 1980s film look, handheld, slow push-in. He listens on the payphone, tense. The left train rushes past, the roar drowns the call, he frowns and shouts \"Hello? I can't hear you!\" The train leaves, sudden quiet, he hears the voice, exhales and smiles: \"Yeah... I'm here.\" Train wind moves his hair, window light flickers on his face. No text." --duration 5 --resolution 1080p --wait --wait-timeout 20m --json
72: 6. Start a batch. Without --wait, each call returns a job id at once, so a loop over a prompt file starts one job per line.
73: while IFS= read -r prompt; do
74: higgsfield generate create seedance_2_5 --prompt "$prompt" --duration 5 --json | jq -r '.[]' >> job_ids.txt
75: done < prompts.txt
76: The full batch workflow, including how to collect results, is in the scripts section.
77: Commands in this guide were checked on October 16, 2026 with Higgsfield CLI 1.1.26 on macOS. Model ids, parameters and credit prices can change, so use higgsfield model list, model get and generate cost for current values.
78: CLI vs MCP vs API
79: Higgsfield has three programmatic routes. They differ by who calls them and how they are billed, so the choice comes before installation.
80: CLI vs MCP vs API
